content.title: Interesting direction, but poor experiments
content.review:
**Summary:**
The paper introduces an approach for performing tasks in interactive environments. The goal of the paper is improving sample efficiency by incorporating information about multiple objects into Q-value estimation and also discriminating object states according to the interactions. The paper considers 8 types of tasks in the AI2-THOR environment and reports success rate for each of the tasks. The paper also provides the results for a number of baselines and ablation experiments.

**Strengths:**
- The paper explores improving sample efficiency for long-horizon interactive tasks, which is a very interesting direction.
- The ideas for incorporating object relations and states are also interesting.

**Weaknesses:**
The major issue of this paper is the experiments:

(1) The same environment has been used for training and testing. Train and test environments should be separate from each other.

(2) The generalization of the method has not been evaluated since the same environment has been used for train and test. Sample efficiency is important but not without generalization. A large capacity model probably overfits much faster than any of the proposed models and baselines. The issue is that it might not generalize.

(3) Only 1 scene out of 120 scenes of THOR has been used. The paper should consider a larger set for reporting the results.

Other comments:

- The paper claims that the method is unsupervised but a pre-trained model is used for extracting bounding boxes for objects.

- The paper contrasts the method with imitation learning, but it uses groundtruth location information across the trajectory. That is also considered strong supervision.

- I recommend using datasets such as ALFRED (Shridhar et al., CVPR 2020) which includes a variety of tasks and separate train/val/test splits.

- I also recommend using more sample efficient RL techniques such as PPO to see if the proposed method provides any improvement over those or not. 

**Score justification:**
The paper explores a very interesting direction, but the experiments are flawed as explained above. So I choose a reject rating.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Not bad method, but weirdly easy self-made tasks for an embodied agent setting
content.review:
## Summary

The authors are trying to solve single-task object interaction problems in a 3D environment (e.g. "find and slice the lettuce and the tomato"). The proposed method involves learning a Q function for object interactions, a self-supervised attention mechanism, and an auxiliary loss for an object-centered forward model.

## Strengths & Weaknesses

#### Strengths

1) The proposed model performs well in the experiments and reaches a high success rate.
2) I'm not an expert in this specific sub-field of embodied agents but upon skimming the baseline papers, they look like sensible choices.

#### Weaknesses

1) It came as a bit of a surprise to me that the authors created their own tasks for this and how simple the tasks are. I thought in the embodied agent community we had moved to task-/goal-conditioned policies (see e.g. ALFRED [1] and their top contributions on their leaderboard). In this paper, the authors created multiple tasks, but any single agent only has to solve one task, from different starting positions. Maybe I misunderstood something about the task definition, but a simple DQN can learn most of the tasks in 0.5 mil steps with over 80% success rate. I appreciate the contribution in the sense that your network does seem to learn to pay attention to relevant object patches - I had just hoped you would be able to take that and apply it to a new setting, e.g. test if the attention generalizes to the same object in a new apartment/environment.
2) The are some clarity problems that aren't a big deal in themselves but add up to a slightly opaque method. I think these are easier to overcome than my other concern: (a) a network diagram would've been nice. I know there's a table in the appendix, but I think it's crucial that the main paper can stand on its own and it's not entirely clear from the writing, how many networks there are and how they work together. (b) Is Eq.6 the full loss? You're only training on the Q values and the encoding of the objects in the next step? (c.) You removed the task description from 5.1 and put it into the appendix. I don't think this is good practice. If you were using a standard method like OpenAI Gym's HalfCheetah-v2 or something that's common in RL literature, then I would agree that the task description could go into the appendix but since you created these tasks from scratch, I think *the main paper needs to contain information about the tasks that you're evaluating your model on.* (d) Clarity question: The objects are always in the same position and the main difficulty stems from the fact that the agent starts in different starting positions, right? If that's the case, in order to assess the difficulty of the tasks, would you mind adding the success rate of a random agent, please? And what's the average starting distance of the agent from the first required object (in terms of actions, not grid spaces)? (e) Figure one has a bit of a misalignment between the drawing and the caption. The drawing is good, but the caption talks about reusing $\mathcal{R}$ in $f_{model}$ but how that's done is not depicted, $f_{int}$ is only explained in the text later, and you mention computing $Q$ values, but it's not highlighted in the diagram 

**TL;DR how to improve the paper:** Please add more implementation details, as outlined in (2) and if possible, and please comment on how goal-conditioning would work in this setting or report test scores, where you test your trained policy on the same task but in a different configuration (different apartment/different positions of objects).

## Impact & Recommendation

As mentioned above, the method seems fundamentally sound but I have 2 concerns about the impact and novelty: (a) goal-conditioned tasks (i.e. environments where the agent receives varying instructions) seem to be the standard for embodied agent works these days and this paper takes a step back from that and (b) the main selling point of the paper is that it doesn't require expert demonstrations or object supervision but that data is available, so why not use it (see [1] - ALFRED can generate expert solutions for any given task, and there's ShapeNet of course, as well as several other 3D and 2D object segmentation datasets that allow for pretraining)? How is it more realistic to have an embodied agent run the same environment 10,000 times than to pretrain the agent on objects or seed it from a handful of expert demonstrations?

I think that a lot of work has gone into this work. For now, I'd recommend rejecting this work but I hope the authors can shed some light on how they are positioning themselves and how to better motivate this work so that I can raise my score.


## Questions, Nitpicks, and Comments

- I appreciate that you start with an example. Always great. But maybe take a more interesting example than warming up a single potato. :D Do the toast for example. It's a reasonably complex problem: find bread, take bread, find a toaster, insert bread, wait for the bread to finish toasting.
- I don't know if it's clear to everyone that the reward of +1 is only given at the very end of that episode when the bread is golden brown or the potato is hot. There's no intermediate sparse reward for finding the potato/pot/bread/toaster, etc. I think it'd be great to highlight this in the introduction a bit more.
- What does "discriminative across object-states" mean in the intro?
- In section 2: You mention "In contrast, we do not provide the agent with any ground-truth object information" - but you do, you give the agent patches/bounding boxes.
- In section 5.0, you're already giving away the conclusions of your experiments. I'd wait with that until the reader has actually seen the results.
- Fig. 3 you write "Percent Million Frames" on the x-axes but you can skip the "Percent", right? It's just 0 - 0.5 "Million Frames".
- couple of small typos like "...mean success rate success rate" top of page 7.
- Table 1 why does "fill cup with water" performs so well on DQN and why is your method beaten by the most naive baseline here? 
- Section 5.3: "We suspect that this is due to its ability to bootstrap object-attention." - could you explain this, please?


## References

[1] https://askforalfred.com/
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

display_title: Response to main comments and implementation details

content.title: Response to main comments and implementation details
content.comment:
We apologize for the delay in response. We plan to withdraw this submission as criticisms of reviewers that one should utilize available resources when making intelligent agents seem misaligned with our goals of developing intelligent agents that minimally rely on supervision. We comment on this in more detail in our response to all reviewers.

**Main comments**

> It came as a bit of a surprise to me that the authors created their own tasks for this and how simple the tasks are. I thought in the embodied agent community we had moved to task-/goal-conditioned policies (see e.g. ALFRED [1] and their top contributions on their leaderboard). Goal-conditioned tasks (i.e. environments where the agent receives varying instructions) seem to be the standard for embodied agent works these days and this paper takes a step back from that.

The main advantage of goal-conditioning seems to be in a multi-task setting, where a goal specifies a task (e.g. instructions). We agree that this is an interesting direction which we plan to pursue next. 

> Please comment on how goal-conditioning would work in this setting or report test scores, where you test your trained policy on the same task but in a different configuration (different apartment/different positions of objects).

For generalizing a policy to different positions of objects or to new apartments, some mechanism for remembering where the agent has searched would be necessary. This could be done with an RNN for example. We would probably want to give goals as either text instructions or as goal-images. A memory mechanism would be necessary here as well for the same reasons as above. If given as text, attention could be used with the instructions to form subgoals for the agent (e.g. as [2] did). Subgoals could be individual instruction words or spans of text.

> In this paper, the authors created multiple tasks, but any single agent only has to solve one task, from different starting positions. Maybe I misunderstood something about the task definition, but a simple DQN can learn most of the tasks in 0.5 mil steps with over 80% success rate. 

We point out that we are not testing against a simple DQN but one with attention. In our ablation, we show that a simple DQN without attention has a hard time learning these tasks. 

**Implementation Details**

>  (a) a network diagram would've been nice. I know there's a table in the appendix, but I think it's crucial that the main paper can stand on its own and it's not entirely clear from the writing, how many networks there are and how they work together.

Thanks for the suggestion. We will add a network diagram for clarity. We have 4 networks: 1 for encoding full egocentric views, 1 for encoding object-image-patches, 1 for computing Q-values, and 1 for predicting the model output. 

> (b) Is Eq.6 the full loss? You're only training on the Q values and the encoding of the objects in the next step?

Eq 6 is the full loss. We only use the information from the next step for training both Q-values and the object-model.

> (c.) You removed the task description from 5.1 and put it into the appendix. I don't think this is good practice. If you were using a standard method like OpenAI Gym's HalfCheetah-v2 or something that's common in RL literature, then I would agree that the task description could go into the appendix but since you created these tasks from scratch, I think *the main paper needs to contain information about the tasks that you're evaluating your model on.*  

Thanks for the suggestion. We'll put a table of the tasks we study and their characterestics in the main text.

> (d) Clarity question: The objects are always in the same position and the main difficulty stems from the fact that the agent starts in different starting positions, right? If that's the case, in order to assess the difficulty of the tasks, would you mind adding the success rate of a random agent, please? And what's the average starting distance of the agent from the first required object (in terms of actions, not grid spaces)? 

Thanks for the suggestion. We will add results like this in a future version of the paper.

> (e) Figure one has a bit of a misalignment between the drawing and the caption. The drawing is good, but the caption talks about reusing R in fmodel but how that's done is not depicted, fint is only explained in the text later, and you mention computing Q values, but it's not highlighted in the diagram

Thanks for pointing this out. Will improve the diagram.

[1] https://askforalfred.com/

[2] Oh et al. Zero-Shot Task Generalization with Multi-Task Deep Reinforcement Learning, ICML 2017

content.title: Questions, Nitpicks, and Comments
content.comment:
> What does "discriminative across object-states" mean in the intro?

Consider the toaster in toasting bread. The agent should only turn the toaster on once the bread is inside the toaster. So the agent should discriminate a "filled" toaster from an "empty" toaster. Likewise, it should only pickup the bread once the bread is cooked, so it should discriminate "cooked" bread from "uncooked" bread. 

> Section 5.3: "We suspect that this is due to its ability to bootstrap object-attention." - could you explain this, please?

Because our object-model incorporates attention into its predictions, the prediction error is an additional learning signal for learning object-attention. While ground-truth object-information provides oracle features, it does not provide an extra learning signal to speeded learning attention.


> - I appreciate that you start with an example. Always great. But maybe take a more interesting example than warming up a single potato. :D Do the toast for example. It's a reasonably complex problem: find bread, take bread, find a toaster, insert bread, wait for the bread to finish toasting.
> - I don't know if it's clear to everyone that the reward of +1 is only given at the very end of that episode when the bread is golden brown or the potato is hot. There's no intermediate sparse reward for finding the potato/pot/bread/toaster, etc. I think it'd be great to highlight this in the introduction a bit more.
> - In section 5.0, you're already giving away the conclusions of your experiments. I'd wait with that until the reader has actually seen the results.
> - Fig. 3 you write "Percent Million Frames" on the x-axes but you can skip the "Percent", right? It's just 0 - 0.5 "Million Frames".
> - couple of small typos like "...mean success rate success rate" top of page 7.

Thanks for the suggestions. We agree with these points and will change the paper to reflect your suggestions.

> In section 2: You mention "In contrast, we do not provide the agent with any ground-truth object information" - but you do, you give the agent patches/bounding boxes.

Good point. We will clarify this.

>  Table 1 why does "fill cup with water" performs so well on DQN and why is your method beaten by the most naive baseline here?

Good question. The pros of our method are both learning speed & success rate. We still learn more quickly than this naive baseline. We are not sure why we get a lower maximum success rate. We note that they're within a standard deviation of each other.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
- Summary
    - This paper presents an architecture for learning object interaction tasks in AI2 Thor with sparse rewards.  The architecture utilizes attention to select actions with an object centric representation.  To handle reward sparsity, the authors propose an auxiliary objective that predicts the visual state of a given object in the next frame given an action applied as formulate it is a contrastive loss.
    - They evaluate their method on 8 tasks in one scene in AI2 Thor and outperform the baseline methods while also performing similarly to an agent equipped with ground truth object information
- Strengths
    - Proposed method is able to learn under sparse rewards
    - Proposes a novel auxiliary objective for object centric RL
    - Evaluated in a reasonably complex setting
- Weaknesses
    - The evaluation is performed on a single scene and the same scene is used for both training and testing.  The work would be considerably stronger if a train/test split was used and ideally all scene types.
    - "We assume no access to supervision."  I disagree with this claim.  The object detector, while only providing object proposals, was trained on some supervised data.  On what data was the object detector trained (I couldn't find these details in the paper or supplement)?  If it was trained on COCO or similar, an argument could be made that this shouldn't count.  Further, can the authors please confirm that all methods compared benefit from equally from this source of supervision?
    - I would also like to see an ablation as to how the method performs as object detector performance is degraded
    - One weakness with this work is the premise that we should learn with sparse rewards.  In the case of learning in reality, shaped reward may not be available, but when learning in simulation, there is a wealth of information available for reward shaping.  It is unclear to the reviewer if the effort to design an effective shaped reward is any more than the effort to design a model that doesn't need one.  It is also unclear if methods trained with a sparse reward transfer to reality better than those trained with a shaped reward.  Given the limited number of scenes the method was evaluated on, I also cannot assess whether the method is likely to work well in reality.  Given all this, I am left wonder why one should use a sparse reward.
- Overall
    - While the proposed method seems to be effective, the evaluation is limited and there are issues that need to be addressed before publication.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response
content.comment:
>  It is unclear to the reviewer if the effort to design an effective shaped reward is any more than the effort to design a model that doesn't need one. It is also unclear if methods trained with a sparse reward transfer to reality better than those trained with a shaped reward. 

The object-model we develop and study is task-agnostic so it can be applied more widely than shaped rewards. For example, if the agent is in a novel environment where there isn't enough domain knowledge to define shaped rewards, the agent can still learn a model for the objects.

>  Given the limited number of scenes the method was evaluated on, I also cannot assess whether the method is likely to work well in reality. 

Good point. We will test on more scenes to verify this method is scene-agnostic.

> "We assume no access to supervision." I disagree with this claim. The object detector, while only providing object proposals, was trained on some supervised data. On what data was the object detector trained (I couldn't find these details in the paper or supplement)? If it was trained on COCO or similar, an argument could be made that this shouldn't count. 

We agree that we assume this supervision. For this study, we used an oracle detector available in the simulator.

> Further, can the authors please confirm that all methods compared benefit from equally from this source of supervision?

We confirm that all methods had access to oracle bounding boxes provided by the simulator object-detector.

> I would also like to see an ablation as to how the method performs as object detector performance is degraded

Thanks for the suggestion. We will incorporate this.

display_title: Paper achieves good results on the chosen tasks. Why were these tasks the ones chosen?

content.title: Paper achieves good results on the chosen tasks. Why were these tasks the ones chosen?
content.review:
Summary
==========================================
This paper describes a way learn an attention mechanism for objects in a 3D environment without explicit supervision. This attention mechanism allows the proposed network, ROMA, to outperform existing approaches without having access to the ground truth state of the object.

Score
==========================================
Overall, I recommend accepting this paper. My biggest concern is that the tasks performed in the paper lack variety in that they are all kitchen based tasks moving small objects. I am curious about tasks that have further dependencies where both objects may not be visible from the same viewpoint. The paper is well written and it does give results on 8 different tasks even if they are similar. The approach gives empirically good results on the chosen tasks with low sample complexity. I would like to see results on 1 similar, but distinct category of tasks (like simple, single object navigation).

Pros
==========================================
- This paper is able to learn to perform these tasks without imitation learning
- The approach is more sample efficient than the baseline
- Able to learn these tasks with rich object designed feature
- The figures are very clear and readable.
- The paper demonstrates a strong baseline that outperforms unexpectedly OCN.

Cons and Questions
==========================================
- The AI2Thor scenes are small enough that the object is often almost always visible. I wonder if ROMA would be able to perform as well in environments where the ground truth desired objects aren't always visible. Would ROMA learn well if it needed to explore in larger environments?
- How do these tasks compare with those that networks like OCN were intended to be used? I am very surprised OCN does worse than the baseline. Are the authors confident its not a hyperparam problem?
- All of the objects are small hand-held objects, would it be possible to add some experiments using larger objects? I wonder if the attention component of ROMA is so helpful because of the relative size of the objects. Would ROMA perform just as well when one of the objects saturate the agent's field of view? Or is the attention component only helpful when the objects are small as they are in the constructed tasks.
- "We report results on the 8 tasks that had the highest optimal length." What other tasks were evaluated? Why was choosing tasks that had high optimal length important? Does ROMA perform poorly on tasks that have a low optimal length? Is it that ROMA is designed on tasks with high optimal length? 
- This paper clearly demonstrates where ROMA outperforms other techniques (with these compositional object tasks). Which tasks does ROMA under perform on compared to these methods, if any? Do these other techniques perform well when no composition of objects is required?
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

replying_to: Replying to Paper achieves good results on the chosen tasks. Why were these tasks the ones chosen?

content.title: Response
content.comment:
> The AI2Thor scenes are small enough that the object is often almost always visible. I wonder if ROMA would be able to perform as well in environments where the ground truth desired objects aren't always visible. Would ROMA learn well if it needed to explore in larger environments?

We believe so and will run experiments on large environments to verify this. 

> How do these tasks compare with those that networks like OCN were intended to be used? I am very surprised OCN does worse than the baseline. Are the authors confident its not a hyperparam problem?

OCN was trained on tasks where a robot moved around objects but didn't interact with them. As such, OCN only needed to learn view-invariance. Our tasks require an agent interact with objects and learn to represent them as they change in "object-state" (features such as being on vs. off, cooked vs. uncooked, etc.). As such, the agent needs to learn a representation that isn't invariant but in fact *discriminative* of changes in these features so it can recognize a "turned on" toaster from a "turned off" toaster. We hypothesize that OCN's view-invariance is its source of poor performance and confirm in Table 2 than OCN cannot discriminate object-states well.

> All of the objects are small hand-held objects, would it be possible to add some experiments using larger objects? I wonder if the attention component of ROMA is so helpful because of the relative size of the objects. Would ROMA perform just as well when one of the objects saturate the agent's field of view? Or is the attention component only helpful when the objects are small as they are in the constructed tasks.

We believe the utility of the attention is agnostic to object-size and instead shows its benefit when objects must be used together, requiring the agent to attend to multiple objects. Additionally, many "interesting" tasks are those where objects are used together and lead to changes in object-properties (e.g. turning an object hot, wet, on, open, etc.). These typically occur with smaller objects that are used together (e.g. cup get's filled with water in sink). That said, we can add tasks with larger objects in the future.

>  "We report results on the 8 tasks that had the highest optimal length." What other tasks were evaluated? Why was choosing tasks that had high optimal length important? Does ROMA perform poorly on tasks that have a low optimal length? Is it that ROMA is designed on tasks with high optimal length?

Tasks with a higher optimal length are harder to learn because the agent needs to find a longer sequence of actions to complete the task. With shorter tasks, we found that ROMA and other methods all performed comparably well.

> This paper clearly demonstrates where ROMA outperforms other techniques (with these compositional object tasks). Which tasks does ROMA under perform on compared to these methods, if any? Do these other techniques perform well when no composition of objects is required?

Attention and our object-model are less useful when (a) objects don't need to be used together and (b) object-properties don't change. In these instance, ROMA performs equally well to a more naive baseline that doesn't use attention or learn to differentiate object-properties. Example tasks include picking and placing, where the agent simply needs to pick an object up and place it somewhere.

replying_to: Replying to Reinforcement Learning for Sparse-Reward Object-Interaction Tasks in First-person Simulated 3D Environments
display_title: Thank you to reviewers. We will withdraw this submission and strengthen it for our goals of learning without expert demonstrations or shaped rewards

content.title: Thank you to reviewers. We will withdraw this submission and strengthen it for our goals of learning without expert demonstrations or shaped rewards
content.comment:
Thank you to the reviewers for thoughtful and insightful comments. We agree that for practical applications, if one has access to expert demonstrations or to enough domain knowledge to design shaped rewards, one should use this information. While both are available for AI2Thor and learning from this is an interesting endeavour, this not our research goal. Instead, we are interested in developing agents that can learns tasks from a relatively limited amount of interactions with the world when the agent doesn't have access to expert demonstrations or shaped rewards. This may happen if the agent is in a novel environment for which expert demonstrations aren't available, or for which there isn't enough domain knowledge to define shaped rewards. 

We use AI2Thor as a testbed for exploring architectures and objective functions that reduce sample-complexity in object-interaction tasks when expert demonstrations or shaped rewards aren't available. We note that because our core contribution is an object-centric representation learning method that improves sample-efficiency, this research may still be useful for methods that leverage expert demonstrations or shaped rewards. That said, as a first step, we focused on improving training performance because we believe that object-interaction tasks are challenging when one doesn't bootstrap from expert demonstrations or shaped rewards. We thank the reviewers for their insightful comments and suggestions on how we may extend our task suite to better demonstrate the challenges object-interactions tasks and to better study an agent's capability of solving them. We plan to study our agent's ability to generalize its policy as a next step.
